items.title: How it works
items.text: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme involved in DNA structure and repair. DNA damage can stop cancer cells dividing. Healthy blood-forming and other cells can also be affected. Absorption by mouth varies, so oral and intravenous doses are not interchangeable.

items.title: Evidence and limits
items.text: Older studies reported tumour responses with oral etoposide. The evidence is limited, and the different oral schedules cannot be assumed to have the same benefit or risks. A small uncontrolled study of a 21-day oral course does not establish a survival advantage or validate all three NCCP schedules. Its participants had recurrent cancer and substantial treatment toxicity; do not transfer its response percentage to an individual.

items.title: The treatment aim
items.text: This chemotherapy combination aims to control extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer, ease symptoms and help people live longer. Expected benefit depends on the cancer, general health and treatment choices. Ask what the team hopes it will achieve for you.

items.title: The precise regimen
items.text: This guide covers carboplatin plus oral etoposide for extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer in people unsuitable for cisplatin-based treatment. It does not cover an intravenous etoposide schedule or an added immunotherapy medicine. If the prescription differs, ask for its matching guide and consent discussion.

items.title: What the evidence can tell us
items.text: The studies cited by NCCP support platinum–etoposide treatment and provide background on using etoposide by mouth, but they did not test this exact carboplatin plus all-oral three-day schedule. The oral comparison used cisplatin and a mixture of intravenous and oral etoposide. A separate pooled analysis compared platinum choices across several trials. These results cannot give a precise survival estimate for this prescription or predict your individual benefit.

chapters.title: What to watch for
chapters.intro: Tell the team early so symptoms can be assessed and treated.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines can lower blood counts, increasing infection, bleeding or anaemia risk. Attend monitoring and report sudden illness, bruising or bleeding.

items.title: Mouth, stomach and energy
items.text: Sickness, diarrhoea, constipation, mouth soreness, appetite loss, fatigue and hair loss may occur. Ask for help early; inability to drink or persistent vomiting needs urgent advice.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Tell the team about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness, balance problems or reduced urine. Some effects can persist after treatment.

items.title: Less common serious effects
items.text: Serious allergic or skin reactions can occur. Etoposide also carries a risk of secondary leukaemia; ask the team to explain serious and lasting risks in your situation.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use the unit’s 24-hour number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Urgent symptoms
items.text: Call your unit urgently for fever at its stated threshold, shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, unusual or uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Swelling of the tongue/throat or trouble breathing can be an emergency. Report new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty walking promptly.

items.title: What to say when you call
items.text: Give the regimen name, last infusion and capsule dose, symptoms and when they began. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect all the details.

chapters.title: Reviewing the course and next steps
chapters.intro: The number of cycles is a clinical decision.

items.title: Before another cycle
items.text: Attend weekly blood counts as arranged and kidney/liver tests before each cycle. The team reviews toxicity and benefit; do not restart capsules until authorised.

items.title: How long treatment continues
items.text: Carboplatin is planned into a vein on Day 1, before oral etoposide. Etoposide capsules are prescribed twice daily on Days 1, 2 and 3 only, on an empty stomach. The cycle repeats every 21 days while treatment is helping and side effects remain acceptable. Your team decides when to delay, change or stop; the source does not set a fixed number of cycles.

items.title: After a change or stop
items.text: Confirm which medicines stop or continue, how unused capsules are returned, and follow-up for ongoing symptoms. Ask who will contact you about the next treatment or supportive-care plan.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Are oral capsules a weaker form of chemotherapy?
questions.a: No. Etoposide capsules are chemotherapy and can cause serious effects. Their absorption differs from an infusion, so only the treating team can choose or change the dose.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit a dose?
questions.a: If a dose is missed, do not double the next dose or extend the course. The manufacturer leaflet advises taking the next dose when due; inform your oncology pharmacist/team and follow your written plan. If you vomit after a dose, contact the team for instructions rather than automatically taking replacement capsules. BC Cancer specifically advises no repeat dose after vomiting within one hour unless the healthcare team directs it. Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down needs urgent advice.

questions.q: Do I continue capsules every day until the next infusion?
questions.a: No. This regimen prescribes twice-daily etoposide on Days 1–3 only. Use your own written calendar and wait for the team to confirm the next cycle.

questions.q: Will I always have a fixed number of cycles?
questions.a: The current NCCP source continues this regimen until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, with ongoing review. Your team agrees the number of cycles and may stop or change earlier.

risk.mapping_basis: Day 1 high-risk carboplatin; Days 2–3 oral etoposide minimal–low. Select the treatment day; no automatic high-risk plan on capsule-only days.

protocol_metadata.schedule_summary: Carboplatin is planned into a vein on Day 1, before oral etoposide. Etoposide capsules are prescribed twice daily on Days 1, 2 and 3 only, on an empty stomach. The cycle repeats every 21 days while treatment is helping and side effects remain acceptable. Your team decides when to delay, change or stop; the source does not set a fixed number of cycles.
